name: Tyrannosaurus Rex
discoveryHistory:
• First partial skeleton was discovered in 1900 by Barnum Brown in Wyoming.
• Henry Fairfield Osborn formally named the species Tyrannosaurus rex in 1905.
• In 1990, the most complete specimen, 'Sue', was discovered in South Dakota.
interestingFacts: Possessed the strongest bite force of any terrestrial animal.
Had binocular vision providing excellent depth perception.
Its arms were exceptionally small but highly muscular.

name: Velociraptor
discoveryHistory:
• First fossil discovered in 1923 by Peter Kaisen in the Gobi Desert.
• Formally described by Henry Fairfield Osborn in 1924.
• A famous 'Fighting Dinosaurs' fossil showing Velociraptor locked in combat with a Protoceratops was found in 1971.
interestingFacts: It had feathers, proven by quill knobs found on forearm fossils.
Its iconic sickle claw was used for piercing rather than slashing.
It was roughly the size of a modern turkey, not a human.

name: Spinosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in 1912 by Richard Markgraf in the Bahariya Formation of Egypt.
• Ernst Stromer described and named the species in 1915.
• Original fossils were destroyed during a WWII bombing in Munich in 1944.
interestingFacts: Highly adapted for a semiaquatic lifestyle with dense bones for buoyancy control.
Its neural spines formed a large sail that could have been used for display or thermoregulation.
It is the longest known carnivorous dinosaur, surpassing T. rex.

name: Giganotosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1993 by Rubén Darío Carolini in Patagonia, Argentina.
• Formally named Giganotosaurus carolinii in 1995 by Coria and Salgado.
• Additional fragments of a potentially larger individual were found in later years.
interestingFacts: It had highly serrated teeth ideal for slicing flesh.
Possessed an elongated skull with an underdeveloped sense of smell compared to T. rex.
Likely preyed on giant titanosaur sauropods.

name: Carnotaurus
discoveryHistory:
• A nearly complete skeleton was discovered in 1984 in Chubut Province, Argentina.
• Described and named by paleontologist José Bonaparte in 1985.
• Notable for extensive skin impressions revealing scales without feathers.
interestingFacts: Possessed distinctive thick horns above its eyes.
Had extremely short, vestigial forelimbs with no elbow joints.
Adapted for running at high speeds with powerful hind legs.

name: Deinonychus
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in 1931 by Barnum Brown in Montana.
• John Ostrom redefined our understanding of dinosaurs by describing it in 1969.
• Ostrom's study of Deinonychus sparked the 'Dinosaur Renaissance'.
interestingFacts: Its name means 'terrible claw', referring to the large sickle claw on its foot.
Provided crucial evidence for the evolutionary link between dinosaurs and birds.
Often found in groups, suggesting possible pack-hunting behavior.

name: Tarbosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered during a Soviet-Mongolian expedition in the Nemegt Basin in 1946.
• Evgeny Maleev originally named it as a species of Tyrannosaurus in 1955.
• Later reclassified as the distinct genus Tarbosaurus.
interestingFacts: The apex predator of Late Cretaceous Asia.
Had a narrower snout and more rigid jaw than its North American cousin, T. rex.
Possessed the proportionally smallest arms of any tyrannosaurid.

name: Carcharodontosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• First fragmentary fossils discovered in 1924 in Algeria.
• Ernst Stromer named the genus in 1931 after finding more complete remains.
• Like Spinosaurus, the original fossils were destroyed in World War II.
interestingFacts: Its name means 'shark-toothed lizard' due to its jagged teeth.
Lacked binocular vision, having eyes positioned on the sides of its head.
Shared its environment with the giant Spinosaurus.

name: Albertosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in 1884 by Joseph Burr Tyrrell in Alberta, Canada.
• Named Albertosaurus in 1905 by Henry Fairfield Osborn.
• A massive bonebed containing over 20 individuals was found in 1910.
interestingFacts: The bonebed discovery suggests it may have lived and hunted in packs.
Was lighter and faster than the closely related Tyrannosaurus rex.
Grew at a rapid pace, reaching mature size in less than 20 years.

name: Utahraptor
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1991 by a team led by James Kirkland in Utah.
• Officially named Utahraptor ostrommaysi in 1993.
• Additional specimens have since been found trapped in a potential quicksand predator trap.
interestingFacts: The largest known member of the dromaeosaurid family.
Its massive sickle claw could reach up to 9.4 inches in length.
Built for power rather than speed, unlike smaller raptors.

name: Therizinosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• First found in 1948 by a Soviet-Mongolian expedition in the Gobi Desert.
• Originally thought to be a turtle-like reptile due to the giant claws.
• Later identified as a highly derived, herbivorous theropod dinosaur.
interestingFacts: Had the longest known claws of any animal, reaching over 1 meter.
Despite being a theropod, it evolved to eat plants rather than meat.
Possessed a large gut to digest tough vegetation.

name: Oviraptor
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1923 by George Olsen during an expedition to Mongolia.
• Named 'egg thief' because the first fossil was found atop a clutch of eggs.
• Later discoveries proved the eggs belonged to Oviraptor itself, and it was brooding them.
interestingFacts: Had a short, parrot-like beak with no teeth.
Likely possessed a crest on its head, similar to a modern cassowary.
Its brooding posture strongly resembles that of modern birds.

name: Gallimimus
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the early 1960s in the Nemegt Basin of Mongolia.
• Named by Halszka Osmólska and colleagues in 1972.
• Numerous skeletons of varying ages have been found together.
interestingFacts: One of the largest ornithomimid, or 'ostrich dinosaur', species.
Had a toothless beak that may have been used for filtering small food items.
Adapted for high-speed running to escape large predators.

name: Majungasaurus
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in 1896 by a French military officer in Madagascar.
• Originally named Megalosaurus crenatissimus by Charles Depéret in 1896.
• A complete skull discovered in 1996 clarified its classification as an abelisaurid.
interestingFacts: Provides the first unambiguous evidence of dinosaur cannibalism.
Had a distinctive dome on its skull, unique among theropods.
Possessed robust, muscular hind legs but very short arms.

name: Baryonyx
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in 1983 by amateur fossil hunter William Walker in Surrey, England.
• Described in 1986 by Alan Charig and Angela Milner.
• The holotype specimen included fish scales in its stomach region.
interestingFacts: Had a long, narrow snout resembling that of a crocodile.
Its large thumb claw was likely used to hook fish out of water.
Represents one of the earliest known spinosaurid dinosaurs.

name: Acrocanthosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the early 1940s in Oklahoma, USA.
• Named Acrocanthosaurus atokensis in 1950 by Stovall and Langston.
• A nearly complete skeleton 'Fran' was discovered in the 1990s.
interestingFacts: Characterized by tall neural spines along its back and neck.
Likely the apex predator of the Early Cretaceous in North America.
Its tracks have been found alongside those of giant sauropods in Texas.

name: Dromaeosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1914 by Barnum Brown in the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta.
• Named by Brown and Matthew in 1922.
• The type species of the family Dromaeosauridae.
interestingFacts: Had a heavily built skull with a stronger bite force than Velociraptor.
Relied on its jaws rather than its claws to kill prey.
Was one of the first 'raptor' dinosaurs discovered.

name: Troodon
discoveryHistory:
• A single tooth was discovered in 1856 by Ferdinand Vandeveer Hayden.
• Named by Joseph Leidy in 1856, making it one of the first dinosaurs named in North America.
• The genus has been considered a 'wastebasket taxon' due to confusing fossil fragments.
interestingFacts: Had one of the largest brain-to-body size ratios of any dinosaur.
Possessed large, forward-facing eyes, suggesting excellent nocturnal vision.
Its serrated teeth suggest an omnivorous diet.

name: Gorgosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1913 by Charles M. Sternberg in Alberta, Canada.
• Named by Lawrence Lambe in 1914.
• Over 20 skeletons have been found, making it one of the best-represented tyrannosaurids.
interestingFacts: Coexisted with another tyrannosaurid, Daspletosaurus.
Had a lighter and more gracile build compared to T. rex.
Possessed a small horn-like crest in front of its eyes.

name: Daspletosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1921 by Charles Mortram Sternberg in Alberta.
• Dale Russell recognized it as a distinct genus and named it in 1970.
• Some specimens show bite marks from other tyrannosaurs.
interestingFacts: Was heavier and more robust than its contemporary, Gorgosaurus.
Considered by some scientists to be a direct ancestor of Tyrannosaurus rex.
Had proportionally larger teeth than T. rex.

name: Triceratops
discoveryHistory:
• First recognized from a pair of brow horns found near Denver in 1887.
• Othniel Charles Marsh named it Triceratops in 1889.
• One of the most abundant dinosaurs found in the Hell Creek Formation.
interestingFacts: Its large solid frill lacked fenestrae, unlike most other ceratopsians.
Fossil evidence shows it survived attacks from Tyrannosaurus rex.
Its beak was similar to a parrot's, suited for shearing tough vegetation.

name: Protoceratops
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered by the Central Asiatic Expeditions in the Gobi Desert in 1922.
• Described by Walter Granger and W.K. Gregory in 1923.
• Known from dozens of well-preserved skeletons across all growth stages.
interestingFacts: It lacked the large horns typical of later ceratopsians.
May have inspired ancient Greek myths of the griffin.
Has been found preserved in burrows alongside other individuals.

name: Styracosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• The first skull was collected in 1913 by Charles H. Sternberg in Alberta.
• Named by Lawrence Lambe in 1913.
• Bonebeds suggest it lived in massive herds.
interestingFacts: Characterized by a spectacular frill adorned with up to six long spikes.
Its nose horn could grow up to two feet long.
Despite its fearsome appearance, it was a strict herbivore.

name: Pachyrhinosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1946 by Charles M. Sternberg in Alberta, Canada.
• Described and named in 1950.
• The Pipestone Creek bonebed revealed hundreds of individuals.
interestingFacts: Lacked horns on its face, instead having massive bony bosses.
The bosses were likely used in head-butting combat.
Adapted to cold environments, with some fossils found near the Arctic Circle.

name: Centrosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered by Lawrence Lambe in 1904 in Alberta, Canada.
• Lambe named the genus that same year based on incomplete remains.
• Enormous bonebeds in Dinosaur Provincial Park have yielded thousands of bones.
interestingFacts: Had a single large horn on its snout and small hornlets on its frill.
Lived in vast herds, potentially numbering in the thousands.
Many died in mass drowning events while crossing flooded rivers.

name: Chasmosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• First remains found in 1898 by Lawrence Lambe.
• Formally named by Lambe in 1914.
• Multiple species have been identified from the Dinosaur Park Formation.
interestingFacts: Its frill had massive openings (fenestrae) to reduce weight.
The frill was likely brightly colored for display purposes.
Possessed small brow horns compared to later relatives like Triceratops.

name: Psittacosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1922 by the American Museum of Natural History expedition to Mongolia.
• Named by Henry Fairfield Osborn in 1923.
• Hundreds of complete skeletons have been found, making it one of the most studied dinosaurs.
interestingFacts: Preserved fossils reveal it had long quill-like bristles on its tail.
We know its exact color pattern due to fossilized melanosomes.
It swallowed stones (gastroliths) to help grind up tough plant matter.

name: Pentaceratops
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1921 by Charles H. Sternberg in the San Juan Basin, New Mexico.
• Named by Henry Fairfield Osborn in 1923.
• A massive skull was discovered in 1941, one of the largest of any terrestrial animal.
interestingFacts: Its name means 'five-horned face', including its two elongated cheek bones.
Has one of the largest skulls of any known land animal.
Lived further south than many of its northern ceratopsian relatives.

name: Diabloceratops
discoveryHistory:
• The first skull was found in 2002 by Don DeBlieux in Utah's Wahweap Formation.
• Described and named by James Kirkland and colleagues in 2010.
• Represents one of the oldest known centrosaurine ceratopsids.
interestingFacts: Named for the pair of devil-like horns curving up from the back of its frill.
Had a shorter, deeper snout than most other ceratopsians.
Helped prove that early ceratopsids diversified in southern Laramidia.

name: Kosmoceratops
discoveryHistory:
• Found in 2006 by a volunteer in the Kaiparowits Formation of Utah.
• Formally named by Scott Sampson and colleagues in 2010.
• Its discovery shed light on dinosaur endemism in Late Cretaceous North America.
interestingFacts: Possessed 15 distinct horns or horn-like structures on its skull.
Its name translates to 'ornate horned face'.
The frill horns curled completely downward and forward.

name: Zuniceratops
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1996 by eight-year-old Christopher James Wolfe in New Mexico.
• Described and named by Douglas Wolfe and James Kirkland in 1998.
• Provides a crucial evolutionary link between earlier ceratopsians and later giants.
interestingFacts: The earliest known ceratopsian to feature true brow horns.
Lacked a solid frill, retaining a lighter, fenestrated structure.
Shows that large brow horns evolved before massive size in ceratopsians.

name: Sinoceratops
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 2008 in the Shandong province of China.
• Described by paleontologist Xu Xing and colleagues in 2010.
• The first ceratopsid dinosaur ever found outside of North America.
interestingFacts: Features a frill adorned with forward-curving hornlets.
Lacked brow horns, but had a prominent nasal horn.
Its presence in Asia challenged prior theories of ceratopsid migration.

name: Einiosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1985 by Jack Horner in the Two Medicine Formation of Montana.
• Named by Scott Sampson in 1995.
• Found in low-diversity bonebeds, indicating it lived in herds.
interestingFacts: Distinctive for a prominent nasal horn that curved forward like a bottle opener.
Its name means 'buffalo lizard' in the Blackfoot language.
Only adults possessed the heavily curved horn; juveniles had straight ones.

name: Achelousaurus
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1987 by a team led by Jack Horner in Montana.
• Named by Scott Sampson in 1995 alongside Einiosaurus.
• Represents an evolutionary transition between Einiosaurus and Pachyrhinosaurus.
interestingFacts: Had bony bosses on its snout and above its eyes instead of sharp horns.
Named after Achelous, a Greek river deity who had a horn torn off.
Fossils show a clear progression of horn loss within its lineage.

name: Nasutoceratops
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 2006 in the Kaiparowits Formation of Utah.
• Described by Scott Sampson and colleagues in 2013.
• Added to the growing list of unique dinosaurs from the region.
interestingFacts: Featured an unusually short, thick snout.
Possessed curved brow horns that resembled those of modern cattle.
Its deep snout indicates it ate tough, fibrous vegetation.

name: Parasaurolophus
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1920 by an expedition from the University of Toronto in Alberta.
• William Parks named the genus Parasaurolophus in 1922.
• Extremely rare, with only a handful of good skulls known.
interestingFacts: Its massive crest contained complex, looping nasal passages.
Could use its crest to produce loud, low-frequency sounds for communication.
Once incorrectly thought to use its crest as a snorkel.

name: Iguanodon
discoveryHistory:
• First teeth discovered by Gideon Mantell in Sussex, England, around 1822.
• Formally named in 1825, becoming the second dinosaur ever named.
• Over 30 complete skeletons were discovered in a Belgian coal mine in 1878.
interestingFacts: Featured a large, conical thumb spike used for defense or foraging.
Originally reconstructed as a heavy, sprawling lizard with the spike on its nose.
Could walk efficiently on both two legs and four.
sizeNotes: One of the first dinosaurs named.

name: Edmontosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• First remains were found in the late 19th century during the Bone Wars.
• Lawrence Lambe named the genus Edmontosaurus in 1917.
• Some of the best-preserved dinosaur mummies belong to this genus.
interestingFacts: Fossilized 'mummies' show detailed skin impressions and even a fleshy head comb.
Replaced its teeth continuously in a massive dental battery.
Was one of the main prey items for Tyrannosaurus rex.

name: Corythosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1912 by Barnum Brown in Alberta, Canada.
• Named Corythosaurus by Brown in 1914.
• Early specimens featured extensive skin impressions.
interestingFacts: Its large, plate-like crest resembled a Corinthian helmet.
The crest was hollow and likely used for vocalization.
Lived alongside a vast diversity of other hadrosaurs.

name: Maiasaura
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1978 by Marion Brandvold in the Two Medicine Formation of Montana.
• Jack Horner and Robert Makela named it Maiasaura in 1979.
• 'Egg Mountain' yielded nests, eggs, embryos, and juveniles.
interestingFacts: Provided the first solid evidence that dinosaurs cared for their young.
Hatchlings stayed in the nest and were fed by parents until they grew strong.
Lived in massive nesting colonies, much like modern seabirds.

name: Tsintaosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1950 in Shandong Province, China.
• C.C. Young named the genus in 1958.
• Its distinctive crest was initially thought to be an artifact of preservation.
interestingFacts: Early reconstructions gave it a unicorn-like spike pointing directly up.
Recent studies show the crest was actually part of a larger, paddle-like structure.
Was one of the most prominent hadrosaurs in Late Cretaceous Asia.

name: Lambeosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• First materials collected in 1902 by Lawrence Lambe.
• William Parks named it Lambeosaurus in 1923 in honor of Lambe.
• Has had a complicated taxonomic history with many species consolidated over time.
interestingFacts: Possessed a bizarre crest shaped like a hatchet with a backward-pointing prong.
Its crest was hollow, serving as a resonating chamber.
Crest shape varied significantly based on age and sex.

name: Muttaburrasaurus
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1963 by Doug Langdon near Muttaburra in Queensland, Australia.
• Named by Alan Bartholomai and Ralph Molnar in 1981.
• Is one of the most complete dinosaur skeletons ever found in Australia.
interestingFacts: Had a distinctive, hollow, bony bulge on its snout.
Could likely walk on either two or four legs.
Unlike many iguanodontians, it lacked a well-developed thumb spike.

name: Ouranosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1965 by French paleontologist Philippe Taquet in Niger.
• Formally described and named in 1976.
• Found in the same geological formation as Spinosaurus.
interestingFacts: Characterized by elongated neural spines forming a prominent sail on its back.
Its sail may have been used for thermoregulation or display.
Had a specialized thumb spike and a flattened, duck-like bill.

name: Saurolophus
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1911 by Barnum Brown in Alberta, Canada.
• Named in 1912 by Brown.
• A second species was discovered in Mongolia in the 1940s.
interestingFacts: One of the few dinosaur genera found on multiple continents (North America and Asia).
Had a solid, spike-like crest extending backward from its skull.
Skin impressions suggest a frill running down its back.

name: Olorotitan
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1999 in the Amur Region of Far Eastern Russia.
• Named in 2003 by Pascal Godefroit and colleagues.
• Its skeleton was exceptionally complete for an Asian hadrosaur.
interestingFacts: Possessed a large, hatchet- or fan-shaped hollow crest.
Had a very long neck with 18 vertebrae, more than most hadrosaurs.
Its discovery proved that lambeosaurines diversified in Asia late in the Cretaceous.

name: Shantungosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in 1964 in the Shandong Peninsula of China.
• Named and described in 1973 by Hu Chengzhi.
• Five massive bonebeds have been found, yielding thousands of bones.
interestingFacts: The largest known non-sauropod dinosaur, reaching up to 16.6 meters in length.
Its skull alone was over 1.6 meters long.
Lacked a cranial crest despite its immense size.

name: Tenontosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1903 during an American Museum of Natural History expedition in Montana.
• Formally named in 1970 by John Ostrom.
• Common in the Cloverly and Antlers Formations.
interestingFacts: Its tail accounted for nearly two-thirds of its total body length.
Frequently found alongside the teeth and skeletons of the predator Deinonychus.
Maintained a network of strong ossified tendons along its spine and tail.

name: Hypsilophodon
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in 1849 on the Isle of Wight, England.
• Described in 1869 by Thomas Henry Huxley.
• Early reconstructions incorrectly portrayed it living in trees.
interestingFacts: Was a small, highly agile bipedal runner.
Had a specialized beak for snipping off vegetation.
Maintained a stiff tail for balance while running.

name: Thescelosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1891 by John Bell Hatcher in Wyoming.
• Named by Charles W. Gilmore in 1913.
• Known from several exceptionally preserved skeletons.
interestingFacts: A specimen dubbed 'Willo' was once thought to contain a fossilized heart.
Had a surprisingly heavy build with robust legs.
Possibly dwelled near rivers and streams.

name: Ankylosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in 1906 by Barnum Brown in the Hell Creek Formation of Montana.
• Described and named by Brown in 1908.
• Complete skeletons are rare, with most finds consisting of armor plates.
interestingFacts: Its body was covered in thick bony armor plates called osteoderms.
Possessed a massive tail club capable of shattering bone.
Its broad snout was perfectly adapted for grazing on low-lying plants.

name: Edmontonia
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the 19th or 20th century.
• Holotype found in Cretaceous fossil beds.
• Named Edmontonia by paleontologists after careful study.
• Subsequent discoveries expanded our understanding of its anatomy.
interestingFacts: Edmontonia was a prominent species of its time.
It exhibited unique adaptations to its environment.
Fossil evidence suggests it played a key role in its ecosystem.

name: Pachycephalosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• First remains found in the 1850s, consisting of a skull dome.
• Named in 1943 by Charles W. Gilmore.
• Found mostly in the Lance Formation and Hell Creek Formation.
• Originally thought to be a type of ankylosaur due to the thick skull.
interestingFacts: Featured a domed skull up to 10 inches thick.
May have used its head for flank-butting or intraspecific combat.
Close relative to Stygimoloch and Dracorex, which might be juvenile forms.

name: Isisaurus
dietDetails: High-browsing herbivore feeding on trees and shrubs in Cretaceous forests.
discoveryHistory:
• The fossils were first described and named Titanosaurus colberti in 1997 by Sohan Lal Jain and Saswati Bandyopadhyay.
• In 2003, paleontologists Jeffrey A. Wilson and Paul Upchurch reclassified the remains into the new genus Isisaurus.
• The genus name is an acronym for the Indian Statistical Institute (ISI) in Kolkata, where the fossils were studied.
• The species name colberti honors Edwin H. Colbert, a prominent American paleontologist.
interestingFacts: Had unusually long forelimbs compared to its hindlimbs, giving it a sloped posture similar to a giraffe.
Fossilized dung (coprolites) attributed to Isisaurus contains tree-leaf fungi, confirming it high-browsed forest canopies.
Known from relatively well-preserved fossil remains compared to most highly fragmented Indian sauropod finds.
sizeNotes: Reached an estimated length of 18 meters and weighed roughly 15 metric tonnes.

name: Rajasaurus narmadensis
dietDetails: Apex predator preying on large titanosaurian sauropods and ornithopods in Cretaceous floodplains.
discoveryHistory:
• Unearthed between 1981 and 1983 by Geological Survey of India (GSI) geologists G.N. Dwivedi and Dhananjay Mohabey near Rahioli, Gujarat.
• Excavated under the leadership of GSI paleontologist Suresh Srivastava, who recovered a nearly complete braincase and associated skeleton.
• Formally described in 2003 by a joint Indian-American team including Paul Sereno and Jeffrey A. Wilson after two decades in storage.
• Designated as the holotype GSI Type No. 19/999, providing crucial evidence of abelisaurid distribution on southern landmasses.
interestingFacts: Possessed a unique bony horn on its forehead formed by the fusion of its nasal and frontal bones, used potentially for display or head-butting.
Lived in a highly volcanic, lake-dotted floodplain environment that also served as a massive communal nesting ground for various dinosaur species.
Had extremely short, stubby arms and a robust neck, similar to other abelisaurids like Carnotaurus, suggesting it relied on its powerful jaws for hunting.
sizeNotes: Consensus length of 6.6 to 7.4 meters and weight of 1.5 metric tonnes, standing about 2.4 meters tall at the hip.

name: Jainosaurus
dietDetails: High browser feeding on Cretaceous foliage.
discoveryHistory:
• First fragmentary femur found near Jabalpur in 1871 by Henry Benedict Medlicott of the Geological Survey of India.
• More complete remains were excavated between 1917 and 1920 by British geologist Charles Alfred Matley.
• Initially described by Friedrich von Huene and Matley in 1933 as a species of the South American genus Antarctosaurus.
• Formally moved to its own genus, Jainosaurus, in 1994, honoring Indian paleontologist Sohan Lal Jain.
interestingFacts: Distinguished from other titanosaurs by a tall, distinctive nuchal crest on its braincase.
Initially disputed as a synonym of Titanosaurus before being validated as a distinct genus in 2009 by Jeffrey Wilson.
Its fossils were found preserved in mottled nodular limestone typical of Late Cretaceous India.
sizeNotes: Estimated at 18 meters long and standing 6 meters tall.

name: Indosuchus
dietDetails: Carnivorous predator of small to medium-sized dinosaurs.
discoveryHistory:
• Collected between 1917 and 1919 by British geologist Charles Alfred Matley near Jabalpur, Madhya Pradesh.
• Formally named by German paleontologist Friedrich von Huene in 1932.
• Described in detail by Huene and Matley in a joint monograph in 1933.
• Originally classified as an allosaurid, then a tyrannosaurid, before modern analysis confirmed it as an abelisaurid.
interestingFacts: Had a highly specialized narrow skull roof with frontals and parietals fused, forming a prominent crest.
Coexisted with other abelisaurids like Rajasaurus and Indosaurus, suggesting niche partitioning among Cretaceous Indian carnivores.
Its holotype specimen GSI K27/685 went missing from the GSI collections, making it a subject of taxonomic debate.
sizeNotes: Estimated to be roughly 6 to 7 meters in length and weighing 1.2 metric tonnes.

name: Indosaurus
discoveryHistory:
• Holotype specimen GSI K27/565 was discovered by Charles Alfred Matley at Bara Simla hill, Jabalpur.
• Formally described and named by Friedrich von Huene and Charles Matley in 1933.
• The specific epithet matleyi honors Matley for discovering the rich fossil-bearing beds of the Lameta Formation.
• The original skull roof holotype specimen is currently lost, leading some to consider it a nomen dubium.
interestingFacts: Had an unusually thick skull roof compared to other theropods, showing extreme bone density.
Its classification was disputed for decades, being linked to Megalosaurus before modern placement in Abelisauridae.
Biomechanical analyses suggest it could have had a specialized display structure or horn similar to Rajasaurus.
sizeNotes: Speculative length of 7 to 8 meters based on referred hindlimb elements.
